sections.heading: Asking you to help me pray honestly
sections.text: God, I cannot even come to you rightly unless your Spirit helps me. Teach me how to speak to you from the truth, not from hiding or pretending. I have nothing in myself that can earn your welcome. Let Jesus stand for me. I do not come because I deserve mercy; I come because you are merciful, and because you are full of grace for people who are empty and needy.
theological_themes: Dependence on the Holy Spirit in prayer
Christ's righteousness as the believer's only confidence before God
Approaching God by mercy and grace, not personal merit

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that the Spirit helps believers in their weakness, including weakness in prayer. This supports the opening request that God himself enable truthful communion with him.
Paul rejects any righteousness of his own and wants to be found in Christ with righteousness from God through faith. That grounds the prayer's appeal to Jesus' merit rather than personal worth.

sections.heading: Telling the truth about what is in me
sections.text:
I confess my sin to you — not just the sins I notice once in a while, but the repeated ones, the chosen ones, the ones I return to even when I know better. Sin has touched my thoughts, desires, words, habits, and body. There is a deep spring of corruption in me that I cannot clean by myself.

You see the hidden rooms of my heart: the ugly images I entertain, the dangerous thoughts I wander into, the parts of my fallen nature I have studied and indulged instead of fleeing. I am ashamed of what I am apart from your grace.
theological_themes: Confession of repeated and wilful sin
The corruption of the whole person by sin
God's knowledge of the hidden heart
Shame before God without self-excuse

scripture_references.connection: Jesus locates evil not merely in outward behavior but in the human heart, from which sinful thoughts and actions proceed. This directly supports the prayer's honest naming of inward corruption.
John warns against denying sin and calls believers to confess it before God. The prayer follows that pattern by refusing self-deception and bringing sin into the open before him.

sections.heading: Admitting my barrenness apart from you
sections.text:
Left to myself, I am not alive and fruitful. I am like a plant that only grows thorns, like a leaf already drying up and blown around by the wind, like a winter tree with no fruit to offer. I deserve your judgment. If you dealt with me only according to what I am in myself, I would have no answer.

Lord, will you have mercy on me?
theological_themes: Human barrenness apart from grace
The seriousness of sin under God's judgment
A plea for mercy rather than self-defense

scripture_references.connection: Isaiah describes human uncleanness and compares people in sin to a fading leaf carried away. This gives biblical shape to the prayer's image of spiritual barrenness and helplessness.
Jesus' parable of the unfruitful fig tree shows the seriousness of fruitlessness before God while also leaving room for patient mercy. That tension matches the prayer's confession and plea.

sections.heading: Receiving the blow that breaks my pride
sections.text:
You have struck hard at my pride and at the false god of myself. You have shown me that I cannot be my own savior, my own master, or my own reason for living. I feel broken before you, but this breaking is mercy if it brings me to Christ.

You have given me another Lord: your Son, Jesus. Turn my heart more and more toward holiness. Aim my life toward full obedience to you, like an arrow released from the bow and sent straight toward its mark.
theological_themes: Pride exposed and humbled by God
Self as an idol being dethroned
Christ as Lord and Master
A new direction toward holiness and obedience

scripture_references.connection: Jesus calls anyone who follows him to deny self, take up the cross, and lose life for his sake. This supports the prayer's movement from self-rule to the lordship of Christ.
Paul describes believers as having been set free from sin and made obedient from the heart. That fits the prayer's desire for a heart turned toward holiness under Christ's mastery.

sections.heading: Asking you to kill sin and show Christ in me
sections.text:
Help me in everything I do to resist sin, cut it down, and humble my pride. Save me from loving this world in the way my fallen heart wants to love it — from craving what it offers, needing its approval, and boasting in myself.

Let the character of Christ be seen in me day by day. Make me less ruled by what is natural to sinful humanity, and more shaped by the life of Jesus.
theological_themes: Putting sin to death
Resisting worldliness and pride
Daily growth in Christlikeness
Dependence on grace for sanctification

scripture_references.connection: Paul commands believers to put to death what belongs to the earthly nature and to put on the new self being renewed in God's image. This grounds the prayer's request for active resistance to sin and growth in holiness.
John warns believers not to love the world or its desires, including pride in possessions and status. This directly supports the prayer's request to be saved from worldly love and the pride of life.

sections.heading: Letting you reshape me for Christ forever
sections.text:
Give me grace to accept your will without grumbling. Teach me not only to endure your shaping, but to welcome it. Chisel away what does not belong. Square and fit me for what you are building. Break me loose from the old stone where I have been stuck for so long.

Lift me out of the quarry into the open air of your grace, and build me into Christ forever.
theological_themes: Submitting to God's will without complaint
God's painful but purposeful shaping of the believer
Separation from the old life
Being built into Christ for eternity

scripture_references.connection: Hebrews describes God's discipline as painful yet purposeful, producing holiness and righteousness in his children. This supports the prayer's request to receive God's shaping without resentment.
Peter pictures believers as living stones being built into a spiritual house through Christ. This illuminates the prayer's quarry and building imagery without reducing it to a mere metaphor.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original uses very strong language about human corruption and barrenness. I preserved its Augustinian/Reformed emphasis on sin's depth, while clarifying with phrases like 'left to myself' and 'apart from your grace' so it does not imply that God's saving work in a believer is nonexistent.

The line about being 'fit to be hewn down and burnt' evokes divine judgment and could sound severe to modern readers. I kept the force of deserved judgment while expressing it as a confession before God's mercy rather than as despair.

The prayer's language of God striking pride and chiselling the believer assumes God's providential, sanctifying use of painful conviction and discipline. That can be pastorally sensitive, so I rendered it as God's merciful breaking of pride and purposeful shaping, not as arbitrary harshness.
significant_interpretive_choices: I interpreted 'May thy Spirit speak in me that I may speak to thee' as dependence on the Spirit for honest prayer, not as new revelation or inspired speech equal to Scripture.
I treated 'the merit of Jesus' primarily as the believer's standing before God in Christ, so the modern version emphasizes Christ standing for the sinner and cites justification language.

I kept the original's concrete images of hidden rooms, a barren winter tree, an arrow, chiselling, quarry stone, and being built in Christ, but recast them in contemporary sentence rhythms so the prayer remains natural rather than antique.
I interpreted 'Christ's nature be seen in me' as daily Christlikeness by sanctification, not as a claim that the believer possesses Christ's divine nature in an ontological sense.
